prs.title: Run the fix loop in CI

description.text: Closes #77
From #77's "Do" and "Done when":

- **First, the fixer runs by hand on a real PR.** That's done in #93, on its own PR, for up to three rounds (#93, "Do" step 4). Done on #109: three fix rounds, and six reviews in all. Write up what it did in this issue's PR. Joe doesn't need to look before the job is built. Still untested: whether the fixer acts on a reply from Joe that asks for a fix. That needs Joe, so leave it for him, and say so in the PR.

- **Make the changes the settled open questions above say,** as code review design 4.5 to 4.7 now describe them (written in by PR #108): the fixer's answer shape, the deny rules for the config files, the reviewer's `status` and the backstop check, and when the fix job runs. Check the sandbox's placeholder files in CI, with the fix job's Claude Code version, against the list in `.gitignore`.
- Give the fix job the fixer app's token, from #92.
- Start the fix job's `--allowedTools` from the list #76's replays used. Leave out `Bash(npx tsx:*)`.
- Turn off Claude Code's attribution in the fix job's `--settings`: `"attribution": {"commit": "", "pr": "", "sessionUrl": false}`.
- Add the fix job, the cap of three fix rounds, and the "ready for Joe" label to the "Code review" workflow.
- Run the loop on real PRs.
**Done when:** A PR goes through the loop and gets the "ready for Joe" label, and its runs' transcripts are saved.
**Done.** This PR went through the loop in [run 39852268146](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39852268146), at 54f1fc3, and got the "ready for Joe" label.
- **The review job** posted 3 findings: 1 marked "fix" (F6), and 2 notes (NF5, NF2). Its counts were `fix=1`, `asked=0`, `fixer-commits=0`. Cost: $1.62 at API prices.

- **The fix job** ran the fixer, which answered "needs attention" on the F6, since its fix is in the workflow file, and the fixer can't change one. It made no commit, so nothing was pushed. The posting step replied on the thread and posted the summary comment. No command was refused. Cost: $0.54.
- **The ready job** added the label, since the fixer pushed nothing.
- **Transcripts:** the run's artifacts, `review-transcript-1` and `fix-transcript-1`, kept 30 days.
**The second run,** [39855660869](https://github.com/nimbusscale/road-trip-agent/actions/runs/39855660869), at e7e6eed, after the F6 was fixed by hand:
- **The unready job** took the label off at the start.

- **The review** answered "done" with no findings, and said the F6 fix works. But one of its commands was refused, so the backstop in code review design 4.7 failed the step. It was a false alarm, since the reviewer had read the PR. Joe accepted the backstop as it is (#115). Cost: $1.42.
- **The fix and ready jobs** were skipped, so the label stayed off.
No fix round has pushed yet, so the loop going on after a fixer push hasn't run in CI. The fixer acting on a "fix it" reply from Joe is untested too (#114).
- `npm run check` passes.
- **Both reviews read the rubric, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, and `design/README.md` in full,** with the Read tool, as their first three steps.
- **The sandbox's empty files in CI,** with Claude Code 2.1.308 and the fixer's settings, from a one-off job since taken out. There were 26, all ignored by `.gitignore`, and none untracked.
- **The fixer's transcript:** it ran `fix-input.ts` and `check-fix.ts` with `node --import tsx` in the sandbox, and read the rubric, `DEVELOPMENT.md`, the design doc, and the workflow.

decisions.text: The open questions were settled in chat before this PR, and written in by #108, #111, and #112. These are the decisions made while building it.

- **The fix job pins Claude Code 2.1.308.** The review job stays on 2.1.301. 2.1.308 is the version the fixer, the deny rules, and the sandbox's empty files were tested with. Code review design section 2.
- **Only the review job is in the concurrency group.** If the whole run were in it, the fixer's own push would start a run that cancels the fix job that pushed. Code review design section 4.6.

- **The fix job pushes last,** after it posts the replies, resolves threads, and updates the summary. The push starts the next review, and that review reads the replies' markers. `postFix()` in `fix-post.ts` does the writes in that order. Code review design section 4.5.

- **The fixer never holds a token that can push or post on the PR.** The fix job makes two tokens from the fixer's app. The fixer's token can read code and the PR, and write issues. The posting step's token, made after the fixer ends, can push and post. The checkout doesn't keep the job's own token. Code review design section 4.6.

- **The fixer is also denied `.claude/skills/**` and `.github/workflows/**`.** The fixer's app can't push a workflow file, so a fix there would be posted as "Fixed" and then fail at the push. The skill files were already off limits (settled in #77). The deny rule also stops `sed` from changing one. A fix in either needs attention. Code review design sections 3.6 and 4.5, and the `fix-pr` skill.

- **A wildcard deny rule stays, next to the files it expands to.** For example, `Edit(tsconfig*.json)` stays, along with `Edit(tsconfig.json)`. The sandbox skips the wildcard rule, but the Edit and Write tools still follow it. So they can't create a new matching file. `deny-rules.ts`.
- **A fixer that stops fails the fix job,** so the PR doesn't get the "ready for Joe" label. Code review design section 4.6.

- **Each run takes the "ready for Joe" label off when it starts,** in a job of its own, and only the ready job puts it back. Before, only a fixer push took it off, so a push by Joe left it on a commit whose review could still fail. From the first review's F6, agreed with Joe in chat. Code review design section 4.6.

- **`web/tsconfig.json` has an ask rule now,** `Edit(/web/tsconfig.json)` in `.claude/settings.json`. So the fixer's deny rules cover it too. `Edit(/tsconfig*.json)` covers only the repo root. Joe approved the change in chat.

- **The review job's "fix" count is the findings marked "fix" on the PR's head that have no fixer reply yet.** `round-counts.ts` counts them the same way `fix-input.ts` picks the fixer's findings. So the two always agree. Code review design section 4.6.

- **The sandbox's empty files were checked in CI** with a one-off job, since taken out. It found 26, all of them covered by `.gitignore`. 15 of them stay after the run ends. Code review design section 4.6.

- **Untested: whether the fixer acts on a reply from Joe that asks for a fix.** That needs Joe, so it's left for him (#77, "Do"). To test it, reply "fix it" on a finding the fixer marked "needs attention", then re-run the PR's latest "Code review" run.

- **The fixer's commands could still create a new `eslint.config.js`.** The sandbox skips the wildcard rule `eslint.config.*`, so only the existing `eslint.config.mjs` is read-only for commands. ESLint reads `eslint.config.js` first, so a new one would replace our rules. The commit would show it, and the next review would see it. An exact ask rule for `Edit(/eslint.config.js)` wouldn't help. The sandbox would then make an empty `eslint.config.js` while each command runs, and ESLint would read that instead. An exact deny rule wouldn't help either, for the same reason. Accepted by Joe in chat, since the deny rule `Edit(eslint.config.*)` already stops the Edit and Write tools from creating the file.

prs.title: The itinerary view

description.text: - Add an endpoint that returns the itinerary for the browser, including route lines for the map.
- Show the itinerary beside the chat: the trip summary, stays, legs, and each day's schedule with its free time and rest days. Selected places show their rationale. Refresh the view after each turn.
- On the deployed site (systems design, section 7), the San Francisco skeleton and Day 1 show as in domain model section 5.1.
Closes #57

**On the deployed site: passed.** Checked after the merge and deploy, as Claude's user, on the trip page of `trip_9tbqyu66` (session `session_wjszges7`), where the coordinator had built the San Francisco skeleton and laid out Day 1 with the five places the user named.
- The summary gives May 13 to 15, 2027, San Francisco to Mike's house, 3 days, 2 stays, and 9 h 24 m of driving. The stays are Monterey and San Luis Obispo, one night each.

- Day 1 runs San Francisco → Monterey, starts at 8:00 a.m., and shows its drive (130 mi) and stops along the way. Its stops arrive at 8:30 a.m. (Millbrae Pancake House), 10:05 a.m. (Hangar One), 12:30 p.m. (Philz Coffee), 2:17 p.m. (Santa Cruz Beach Boardwalk), and 7:00 p.m. (Whaling Station, set time), close to domain model 5.1's 8:25, 9:50, 12:05, 1:55, and 7:00. Then 42 minutes of free time before the drive to dinner, and the arrival in Monterey at 8:08 p.m. Each place opens to show its rationale and "You named this place."
- Day 3 shows "Fastest route, as you asked", with the user's reason.

**In the tests: passed.** `src/api/itinerary-view.test.ts` builds the view from the San Francisco example (domain model 5.1). The summary, both stays, Day 1's leg, and Day 1's stop times (8:25, 9:50 a.m., 12:05, 1:55, 7:00 p.m.) match the example. Day 3 shows "fastest" with the user's reason. The Moab example's rest day shows with no leg. The route gives the owner the view in the shape the browser parses, and refuses another user.
**Checked by hand, locally:** the real API against the local Postgres, on #56's San Francisco trip (`trip_gybnhkaj`), with the front end in headless Chrome.
- The chat page shows the itinerary beside the chat, and the trip page shows it under the sessions.
- Day 1 shows its leg, each drive and stop with its times, the free time before the 7:00 p.m. dinner, and the arrival in Monterey. Each selected place opens to show its rationale.
- Day 3 shows "Fastest route, as you asked", with the user's reason.
- Sending "Please start Day 2 at 9 a.m. instead" from the page changed Day 2 to "Starts at 9:00 a.m." when the turn ended, with no reload.
**`npm run check`** passes.

decisions.text: None of these is written into a design doc. Say if one should be, such as the endpoint in systems design section 4.
- **The endpoint is `GET /api/trips/<trip ID>/itinerary`.** It checks the user owns the trip, as the other trip routes do. It's a read, so it works on a started trip too.
- **Each place comes with its latitude and longitude, and each leg with its route line.** So the map (#58) needs no change to the endpoint.

- **Times and durations come from the server as text,** such as "8:25 a.m." and "1 h 20 m". They're written by the same functions as the coordinator's tools, so the view and the chat give the same times. Dates come as ISO text, and the browser writes them in US format, such as "Thu, May 13, 2027".
- **Each leg shows at the top of its day,** not in a list of its own. Domain model 5.1 draws it the same way, and a separate list would repeat each day's ends.
- **A leg's drive time is without the drive buffer,** as domain model 3.8 says. The drives in the schedule include it, since they space out the times.
- **"Stops along the way" lists the day's selected stops whose search area is along the leg.** A breakfast near the hotel, before the drive, isn't listed. Every stop still shows in the schedule.
- **The trip page shows the itinerary too,** under the sessions. Once a trip starts, its chat is closed, so that's the only place to read the plan.
- **A selected place opens on a click to show its rationale.** Under it is the source link, or "You named this place." for a place the user named.
- **The view's reads after each turn share one hook with the memory panel,** `useApiAfterEachTurn()` in `web/src/use-api.ts`. The panel's own copy is gone.
- **`ChatDependencies` gets the settings,** since the calendar needs the drive buffer to work out the schedule.
- Weather and clothing (functional spec 9.6), the map (9.2), and option cards are left to #64, #58, and #62, as their issues say.
- None.

prs.title: The workers' trip tools

description.text: - Add `read_worker_brief_facts` on the `trip` server (tool design 2.1). Reuse `read_itinerary`'s line formatting, so its reply reads like a scoped read.
- Add `add_lodging_candidates` and `add_stop_candidates` on the `trip` server (tool design 2.1).
- Move each stay's activities from `look_up_stay_weather`'s reply to `read_worker_brief_facts`'s stay reply (tool design 2.1 and 2.5). #63 built them into the weather tool, before #191 moved them.
- Leave all three out of the coordinator's definition, which #197 adds. No agent is given them until #60.
- Tests show `read_worker_brief_facts` returns each fact in tool design 2.1 for a stop and for a stay, with the Moab trip (domain model section 5.2), and errors for a check-in and a bad ID.
- Tests show each candidate tool saves a set, and its reply has one line per candidate.
- `look_up_stay_weather`'s reply no longer lists the activities.
Closes #199

- **`read_worker_brief_facts`:** `src/tools/worker-brief-facts-tool.test.ts` reads the Moab trip as planned. For a stay, it checks the town with its place ID, the nights and dates, the lodging candidates already offered, and the activities, including Panorama Point at 1 a.m. on the next date, and the stops along the Torrey day's leg. For stops, it checks the day's ID, number, and date, each stop's kind, purpose, search area, and set time ("none" when it has none), its candidates already offered, and the day's stops in order with their times and selected places. It also checks that two stops on one day share one day's part, and that a stop with nothing offered says so. It errors for a check-in, a day ID, and a stop ID the trip doesn't have.

- **Candidate tools:** `src/tools/candidate-tools.test.ts` saves a lodging set to the Moab stay, a meal set to the Gifford stop along Day 4's leg, with detour times worked out against the leg, and an attraction set near the Torrey stay, with visit times and no detour. Each reply is the set's line, then one line per candidate, and the read shows the new set. It also checks the refusals: a candidate shape that doesn't fit the stop's kind, a place already a candidate, a place given twice, a rejected place, a check-in, and a link that isn't https or http. Each refusal saves nothing, and a repeat is refused before any route is asked for.
- **`look_up_stay_weather`:** `src/tools/weather-tools.test.ts` checks the whole reply, which now ends with the weather lines.

- **Left out of the coordinator's definition:** a test in `src/tools/trip-server.test.ts` checks that the coordinator's definition doesn't list the three tools. `src/agent/coordinator.view.md` is unchanged.
- `npm run check` passes.
Nothing beyond the tests. No agent is sent these tools until #60, so there's no chat to run them in, and they add no SQL.

decisions.text: The issue says "Settled in: chat", but Joe asked for these to be decided without him this time. Each one is here for review.

1. **Notes are a required string, "" when there are none.** Code saves "" as no notes. A tool has no optional inputs (tool design section 4), and an empty string is the plainest "none" for free text. Written into tool design 2.1.

2. **The source link must start with https:// or http://.** The option card links to it, and the link can come from a web page the worker read. A `javascript:` link there could run a script in the user's browser. The error says which links are taken. Written into tool design 2.1.

3. **Each candidate in `add_stop_candidates` is one of two shapes: one with a tier, one with `visitTimeInMinutes`.** Every field in each shape is required. The tool refuses a shape that doesn't fit the stop, and the error says what the stop's kind takes, such as `Day 4, Stop 2 (stop_…), meal: "pie" is a meal stop, so each candidate takes a tier, and no visitTimeInMinutes.` I weighed two other ways. Optional `tier` and `visitTimeInMinutes` would go against "no optional inputs". A `kind` field on each candidate would make the worker pass something code already knows. A candidate with both fields fails the schema. The SDK's error then names the extra key in each shape, which is readable. Written into tool design 2.1.

4. **The candidate tools check the places before they work out any detour time.** A place already a candidate there, a place given twice, or a rejected place refuses the call before any call to Google. A worker asked for "more options" can easily offer an old candidate again, and those Google calls would be wasted. For a rejected place, the error gives the user's reason. The domain still refuses all of these too. Written into tool design 2.1.

5. **What each line of a candidate tool's reply gives.** The first line names the set and the stop or stay as `find_in_trip` names them, such as `Set 2 for Day 4, Stop 2 (stop_…), meal: "pie": 2 candidates.` or `Lodging set 1 for Stay 2, Torrey (stay_…): 3 candidates.` Each candidate line gives the place's name, ID, and short line, its visit and detour times, its rationale, its tier, and its notes. It leaves out how the place was found and the link. Code passes these lines to the coordinator in the worker's result, and a whole read lists no candidates. So the lines are all the coordinator has to talk about the options without a read. The order is the read's: Why, then Tier, then Notes. Written into tool design 2.1, with an example.

6. **How `read_worker_brief_facts` lays out its reply.** Each stay, and each day with stops asked for, is one part, in the order the IDs were given. Stops on the same day share their day's part, and an ID given twice counts once. The reason is size: a Moab stay researcher can be sent six stops on Day 2. One part per stop would list that day's six stops six times. A day's part has three pieces. First comes the read's day line. Then each stop asked for, with its kind, purpose, search area, and set time (always given, as "none" when it has none), and under it the candidates already offered. Each offered candidate shows as its set, its place line, and whether it's selected, with no rationale. Last come all the day's stops, each as a whole read gives its line. A stay's part is the read's stay line, then its lodging candidates already offered, then its activities. Written into tool design 2.1, with an example.
7. **The input is named `stopOrStayIds`,** to match `stopOrStayId` in `select_candidate` and `select_user_place`. Not in a design doc, since it's a field name.
8. **The activities kept the weather tool's wording,** moved as they were, such as `- a hike, no place picked yet: Monday, October 11, 2027, 1:15 p.m.` Not in a design doc.

9. **`read_worker_brief_facts`' description says "Call it first, with every stop and stay ID the worker brief gives, in one call."** Tool design 2.1 says the tool is called first. That's about this one tool, so it goes in its description. #60 can still decide whether the stay researcher's instructions say it too. Not in a design doc, since it's wording.

10. **A check-in gets the same error from all three tools:** `stop_… is a check-in. A check-in has no candidates, so no worker fills it.` The coordinator's error for a check-in tells it to select the hotel for the stay. That doesn't fit a worker. Written into tool design 2.1.

11. **A worker's name for a place is filled in without a word in the reply.** `select_user_place` says when it kept Google's name instead. A worker always passes a name and has nothing to do about it (tool design 2.1), so the line would only add noise. Not in a design doc. Tool design 2.1 already says the name is used only when Google has none.

12. **A worker write's reply is only what the change did.** It gives no leg changes and no check results. Adding candidates doesn't change any selected place, so no leg changes for the worker to report. Not in a design doc. Tool design 2.1 already says these writes return no check results.

- **What the stay researcher's instructions say about each candidate field.** This covers `howFound`, `sourceLink`, the rationale, `notes`, and `visitTimeInMinutes`. The input descriptions give only the format (tool design section 4), so the meaning goes in the instructions. Added to #60's open questions.

- The Moab example (`src/domain/moab-example.fake.ts`) routes Day 1's leg before it sets the Dewey Bridge waypoint. So every write in a test re-routes Day 1 at the finish. It only affects tests. The candidate tests count the routes through the candidates' places, not every route.
None needed.

prs.title: Coordinator prompt and tool description fixes

description.text: - Write a first draft of the new wording for each item, including item 1's itinerary section. Wording given in any item is a starting point, not settled text.
- Make each item's fix in the coordinator's instructions (`src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`), the tool descriptions, and the design doc each one belongs in.
- Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.
- The coordinator's view file shows each item's fix.
- The design docs match the instructions and tool descriptions.
- `npm run check` passes.
Closes #156

- **The coordinator's view file shows each item's fix.** Done. `src/agent/coordinator.view.md` was rewritten with `npm run agent-views` and is in the commit. Its diff shows all 18 items: the new "The itinerary" section, the rewritten "Places the user names" and "Check results" sections, and the changed descriptions of `add_stay`, `update_stay`, `remove_stay`, `update_day`, `set_waypoints`, `update_trip_brief`, `read_itinerary`, `find_place`, and `compute_route`.

- **The design docs match the instructions and tool descriptions.** Done. Functional spec 5.2, technical spec 4.2 and 5.2, tool design 2.1, 2.3, and 2.4, and domain model 4.2 (and one line of 3.4) were changed to match.
- **`npm run check` passes.** Passes: 106 test files, 773 tests. The pre-commit hook ran it too.

decisions.text: This issue is settled in the PR, so these are proposals. All new wording is a first draft for you to review.

1. **Terms and read lines.** New section "The itinerary" in the instructions, after the trip brief and its limits. It defines stay, day, night, last day, rest day, leg, waypoint, stop, candidate, set, search area, road time, and driving with the drive buffer. Then it says what each line of a read means. Dropped the repeat from the reading bullets. Added the section to technical spec 5.2. Reviewed every description against it (see the decisions below for compute_route, set_waypoints, and read_itinerary).

2. **Places the user names.** Rewrote the section into a lead sentence with the reason, then the three cases, from your proposed wording. Changed technical spec 5.2 and tool design 2.1 to match, with the "let's add Arches" example.
3. **When to raise warnings.** Replaced the line with your wording, nearly as given. Changed technical spec 5.2 to match.
4. **add_stay's "after".** `add_stay` and `update_stay` now name `after` and say what "first" does. Added a line to tool design 2.1, "Where an item goes", so `add_stops` and `move_stop` follow it.
5. **"none" for a start time.** Renamed `NO_TIME` to `DEFAULT_START_TIME`, which is "default". Updated `update_day`, its test, and tool design 2.1 (the `update_day` row and "Times are clock times").

6. **find_place's state sentence.** Dropped it from the description. `where`'s input description now says a town or region with its state, or only the state when unsure. Changed the tool design 2.3 row.

7. **What a write's check results list.** The shared trip change rule now also says the already-known results for what the write changed. "Check results" now opens with warning versus note, and what approved and open mean. Changed technical spec 5.2 to match.
8. **Trip memory rule.** Now "Don't save to trip memory what...". Added the bullet to technical spec 5.2, with your 5-hours example to show user memory still gets it.
9. **IDs in chat.** Added a Conduct bullet, and the same to technical spec 5.2's conduct bullet.
10. **"Where the road is still open".** Now "where no stop the user chose already decides the road", in the instructions and technical spec 4.2.
11. **"Saved to the trip".** `find_place` now says every match is stored, so its ID works in the other tools, but that doesn't add it to the itinerary. Same in the tool design 2.3 row.
12. **remove_stay's "near it".** Now "while a stop on another day has this stay as its search area".

13. **Repeats.** Dropped "Stays can't be added until all three are set" from discovery, the rest day rule from "Days and approvals", and "Removing a night always removes the stay's last day" from "Changes to stays". The `tierRule` input now gives only the format. In technical spec 5.2 and domain model 3.4, "the stay's last day" is now "the last of the stay's days".

14. **Refused trip brief update.** Dropped the bullet from the instructions and technical spec 5.2. `update_trip_brief`'s description now says none of the items given is saved, so send the others again. Changed domain model 4.2.

15. **"Unless the route already goes through".** The instructions now say no tool shows a route's road, so judge it from your own knowledge, such as UT-24 through Capitol Reef, and add the waypoint when unsure. Same in technical spec 4.2.
16. **Forgetting a trip brief item.** Added your wording to the end of the trip brief section, and to technical spec 5.2.
17. **Required items.** Added your wording after the item list, with "we don't really have any must-sees" as the example. Same in technical spec 5.2.
18. **"Confirm it and push back".** Now "check that they mean it, and push back", in the instructions, functional spec 5.2, and technical spec 5.2.

- **compute_route's point kinds are now "stopover" and "waypoint",** not "stop" and "passThrough". "Stop" clashed with the itinerary's stop, and "waypoint" is the same idea as a day's waypoints. The description, the error texts, the tests, and tool design 2.4 changed with it. "Destination" was the other name I weighed. It reads oddly for a point in the middle.
- **The shared no-route error now says "Try stopping at one instead",** not "Try one as a stop instead". It comes from both `compute_route` and leg routing, so it can't say "stopover".
- **compute_route and the planning rounds now say "road time",** not "drive time". That's the name the reads and write replies already use.
- **set_waypoints no longer says what a waypoint is.** The new section defines it, so it's said in one place.
- **read_itinerary lost "Schedule times are estimates, from average drive times plus a buffer, and visit times."** That says what the schedule means, so it moved to the new section.
- **update_trip_brief lost "Its feasibility check results also include the trip-wide ones already known."** The shared trip change rule now covers it ("already known for the trip as a whole...").

- **The night arithmetic is said outright:** "a trip's nights add up to one less than its days: a 5-day trip has 4 nights of stays." The examples avoid 6, 12, and 14, since the prompt test treats those as setting values written into the text.
- **Rest day is defined only as "a day with no driving".** Which days can be rest days stays in `update_day`'s description (item 13).

- **The new "The itinerary" section** as a whole. It's about 800 words of the system prompt, which is the biggest addition. I left out lines that explain themselves, such as "Arrives at", the weather line's "Out of date" text, and the rejected places.
- **The "Set" bullet:** "The option card shows only the newest set, so the user can't see an older set's candidates there. When you recommend one of them, name it in chat."
- **The "Places the user names" lead sentence** restates a bit of `read_itinerary`'s description. I kept it because it's the reason the item asked for.

- **`update_trip_brief`'s "none of the items given is saved, so send the others again"** overlaps the shared rule's "If any part is refused, nothing is changed." Item 14 asked to keep it there, as the part that's specific to this tool.

- **`find_place`'s `where` input** now says "when you aren't sure where the place is". That's guidance in an input description, which tool design section 4 usually keeps to format. The item asked for it there.
- **The Conduct bullet on IDs** uses the example "breakfast at Milt's on Day 2".

decisions.text: Calls I made where the issue and the design docs didn't settle it.

1. **run-turn became a library (`src/turn-run/turn-run.ts`).** The experiment runs each turn inside its own process, through the same code `npm run run-turn` uses, rather than starting the script once for each run. `run-turn.ts` is now a thin script over it.

2. **Each run's turn is its own root trace in `road-trip-agent-local`,** not a child of the experiment's task span. That's how a `run-turn` turn looks, so `traceTurnOf` reads it the same way. The task flushes tracing, then reads the turn by its span ID until Phoenix has it.

3. **A case's judge context is built again from the live data,** with `labelerContextOf`, and the dataset refuses a case whose context doesn't match the start of its golden labeler input. So a run is judged on the same `<before>` and `<earlier_turns>` as its golden turn.
4. **No cases file in the repo.** The `saving-replays` dataset in Phoenix is the record, so no trip content goes in the public repo.
5. **A case's golden checks are every check any of its golden saves fails,** since a run's saves don't line up one to one with the golden turn's.
6. **A run that saved nothing isn't sent to the judge.** Its answer is no saves, so it passes, and the `saved nothing` count shows it.
7. **The judge is asked up to 3 times** when its answer doesn't have one entry for each save. After that the run fails, rather than being scored on a wrong answer.
8. **Each run's output keeps its `<turn>`,** so a run can be judged again, such as on a new judge prompt, without running the turn again.
9. **3 turns at a time,** as the candidate refusals evaluation runs. The plan's limit counts tokens, so this sets the speed, not the cost.
10. **The trial was the first case of each of the first 3 sessions,** `trial-1`: 1.1, 1.2, and 1.4.

11. **The report is built from Phoenix, never only at the end of a run.** Every run writes it in a `finally` block, and `replay-report` builds it again. That covered the end-of-run Phoenix disconnect, which happened again on the first baseline run.

12. **`replay-resume` takes a split and a most-runs limit.** A run it leaves out fails at once without starting a turn, so it stays failed for the next resume. This is how the baseline was finished in batches that Joe could watch on the usage meter.

description.text: **Decided by Joe on 2026-11-05, in chat:**

- **What counts as grounded.** A fact in a reply is grounded if it came from any of these:
  - a tool result, from this turn or an earlier turn in the session. This includes trip tool results, such as `read_itinerary`, since code works out much of what they say, such as schedule times, drive times with the buffer, and check results.
  - a worker's result, as the coordinator received it.
  - the user's own words.
  - the coordinator's own knowledge, but only where its instructions allow it, or as a general, guidebook-level description of a well-known place, such as "the Ferry Building is known for its food hall."

Specific facts that can be checked always need a tool result: hours, prices, distances, drive times, addresses, whether a business exists, and current closures. The judge checks where a fact came from, not whether it's true. A made-up opening time fails even if it happens to be right.

- **Where the instructions allow the coordinator's own knowledge.** The rubric copies these two sentences from the coordinator's instructions, in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts`, rather than giving the judge the whole system prompt:
  - From the trip sketches step: "Sketches come from your own knowledge, not from research. … Seasonal closures and hazards also come from your own knowledge at this stage."
  - From the waypoints rule: "No tool shows the road a route takes, so judge that from your own knowledge of the roads, such as UT-24 running through Capitol Reef."

Trade-off: the rubric holds a copy. If the instructions change what the coordinator may say from its own knowledge, the judge keeps grading against the old rule until the rubric is updated by hand. Both sentences last changed on 2026-10-26, before the oldest corpus session (2026-10-30), so the copy holds for the whole corpus.

- **What the judge reads for a turn,** built by code from the turn's spans and the earlier turns in the same session:
  - each user message and reply in the session so far, including the date line.
  - each of the coordinator's tool results, labeled with the tool's name. For the 8 tools whose result doesn't say what it changed, the call's input too: `add_memory_item`, `update_memory_item`, `forget_memory_item`, `update_trip_brief`, `update_itinerary`, `update_day`, `update_stop`, and `update_stay`. Example: `add_memory_item` replies only "Added mem_x to this trip's memory.", so without the input the judge can't check "I've noted that you don't want to see the same thing twice." The input isn't a source for facts. It only shows what a successful change did. Decided by Joe on 2026-11-06, in chat, after the first set.

description.text: Closes #169
- Write the answers to the open questions into the design docs.
- Build it in the domain, the tools, and the itinerary view, with tests using fakes (DEVELOPMENT.md section 5).

- Add the coordinator's rule for when to add one, and how it handles the free time after one (see Decided), in `src/agent/coordinator-prompt.ts` and technical spec 5.2. The implementer drafts the wording, and Joe reviews it in the PR. Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the coordinator's view file with the change.
- A test shows a day like Day 1 above: the drive to the stay, the check-in, the drive to the event, free time before its set time, then the drive back to the stay.
- A test shows the same day with a longer check-in visit time: the party leaves the hotel just in time for the event, with no free time before it.
- Selecting a lodging for the stay moves the check-in to it, and re-routes the leg.
- A test shows the stop-order check splits a day at its check-in: the check-in keeps its place, and only the stops before it, or after it, are reordered.
- `npm run check` passes.

- **Day 1:** `src/domain/check-in.test.ts`, "drives to the stay, checks in, drives to the event, waits there, then drives back to the stay". The day leaves Natick at 10:00 a.m. and reads: the drive to lunch, lunch, the drive to Bar Harbor until 3:57 p.m., the check-in from 3:57 to 4:27, the drive to the college until 4:36, free time from 4:36 to 6:00, the event from 6:00 to 8:00, then the drive back to the stay until 8:09. The leg is routed Lunch place → Bar Harbor → College of the Atlantic → Bar Harbor.
- **Longer check-in:** the next test sets the check-in's visit time to 1 h 54 m. The check-in runs from 3:57 to 5:51, the drive to the college from 5:51 to 6:00, then the event, with no free time.

- **Lodging:** "moves to the lodging once one is selected" selects the Bar Harbor Inn. The check-in's place becomes the inn, and the next `updateLegs()` re-routes Day 1 through Lunch place → Bar Harbor Inn → College of the Atlantic, ending at the inn.

- **Stop order:** "keeps the check-in in its place..." puts lunch and pie before the check-in, and the event and dessert after it. Google is asked for two orders: Natick to Bar Harbor for lunch and pie, and Bar Harbor to Bar Harbor for the event and dessert. The best order is pie, lunch, the check-in, the event, dessert, saving 40 minutes. The stop-order note names the check-in by its place. Another test shows Day 1 itself, with one stop on each side, makes no best-order call.

- Other tests: the refusals (last day, a second check-in on a day, candidates, tier), moving a check-in to the next day, no opening hours result and no "may be too early" mark from a check-in, `add_stops` and `update_stop` with a check-in, the read line, the itinerary view, and the plan document round trip.
- **Checked by hand:** nothing. No SQL changed. The plan document's stop schema now allows an empty search area, and the round trip test covers it with the fake store.
- `npm run check` passes (856 tests).

decisions.text: - **A check-in's search area is empty, not a new search area value.** `Stop.searchArea` is now `SearchArea?`, empty exactly for a check-in. A new value such as `atStay` would have made workers and the search tools treat it as searchable. Written in domain model sections 2 and 3.7.

- **`StopsService.newCheckIn()` creates a check-in.** A check-in always has a visit time, and that comes from a setting, which only the service has. So `add_stops` asks the service for a check-in, and makes a meal or an attraction itself, as before. Written in domain model 4.6.

- **Two new calendar functions:** `placeOf(itinerary, stop)` and `stopPlacesOf(itinerary, day)`. Routing, the schedule's drive times, `hasLeg()`, the checks, the read line, and the itinerary view read a stop's place from them. Written in domain model 4.1.
- **A check-in's `status` is always `selected`.** The "may be too early" mark now goes by status, so a check-in doesn't set it.

- **The stop-order check moved to its own file,** `src/domain/stop-order.ts`, to keep `legs-service.ts` under the line limit. With no waypoints, a part's own drive time is its segments of the leg added up, so it needs no extra call. That matches what the whole-day check did before.
- **`stopsInBestOrder` is empty when no part has two or more stops,** as it was for a day with fewer than two. So Day 1 of the example has none.
- **The read line for a check-in** says "At where the party sleeps that night: Bar Harbor Inn (place_…), Bar Harbor. Visit time 30 m." in place of a search area and a selection.

- **The itinerary view** gets a `checkInPlace` on each shown stop, null except on a check-in. The page shows "Check in, check in and freshen up: Bar Harbor Inn". A check-in gets no map marker, since the stay's marker is already there.
- **`search_near` on a check-in** is refused, with a message that it has no candidates.
- **The `setTier()` refusal now reads** "Only a meal stop has a tier. This one is an attraction." (or "a check-in").
- **The coordinator's new "Check-ins" section,** after "Free time". It covers when to add one, not as the day's last stop, and the free time after one, including a longer check-in visit time.

- **Its example is a Santa Fe day, not Bar Harbor.** #177's evaluation uses a Portland to Bar Harbor day, so a Bar Harbor example could let it pass by copying. Technical spec 5.2 gives the Bar Harbor day and says why the prompt doesn't.
- **A "Check-in" line in "The itinerary" terms,** and the stop line now says "its kind" and that a check-in gives where the party sleeps that night.
- **The `add_stops`, `update_stop`, and `move_stop` descriptions** say what a check-in takes and what's refused.

- **#177's evaluation on Moab Day 4 may see a check-in suggestion.** The new guidance tells the coordinator to suggest checking in before the stargazing. I added an open question to #177 on whether that counts as a pass.
None needed. `settings.json` gains `checkInVisitMinutes: 30`. It's the app's settings file, not one of the config files in DEVELOPMENT.md section 6.

decisions.text: These were made without Joe, as DEVELOPMENT.md section 10 says, though the issue says "Settled in: chat".

- **What a problem and a question are, for `report_result`.** The last open question, settled with its proposal. One block of text, `PROBLEMS_AND_QUESTIONS` in `src/agent/worker-instructions.ts`, that every worker includes word for word. A problem is something the coordinator should know that it can't tell from what the worker saved. A question needs the user's decision, and is asked only when the worker can't do an item well without the answer. Each is a short sentence that names stops and stays as the tools do. The worker doesn't list what it saved, or say all went well. The examples are tool design 2.6's, plus one for "nothing at the tier asked for". **Why:** all three workers share the meaning, and tool design section 4 puts shared rules in one block of code that each prompt includes. Written into technical spec 6.4, with a pointer from tool design 2.6, and struck out in the issue body.

- **The candidate-field block also gives each tier's meaning.** `CANDIDATE_FIELDS` covers `howFound` with `sourceLink`, `rationale`, `notes`, and `visitTimeInMinutes`, as settled, and also `tier`: functional spec 7.1's meanings, by the names the tool takes (`value`, `midRange`, `upscale`), and the price level as a guide. **Why:** `tier` is a candidate field too, and the leg scout labels meals with the same meanings, so it belongs in the block the leg scout reuses. Written into technical spec 6.1.

- **A worker model setting, `workerModel`, set to `claude-sonnet-5-5`.** One setting for every worker. **Why:** a definition with no model can get a default subagent model, so it needs an exact ID, like the coordinator's. Workers judge tiers and fit places to the user's words, which needs more than the smallest model. Several run at once in the fill, so Opus would use up the plan quickly. One setting until an evaluation shows a worker needs its own. Written into technical spec section 10, and the 6.5 bullet on each worker's definition.

- **The coordinator lays out the stops, tells the user, and sends the workers once the user is happy with the stops.** Technical spec 4.2 says the coordinator lays out the stops and then briefs the workers, without saying whether the user sees the stops first. **Why:** a worker run costs searches and model calls, and the functional spec's conduct rule is "don't make choices silently." In the chat check, the user had already said "go ahead", so the coordinator sent them in the same turn. Written into technical spec 5.2, "When to send work to a worker".

- **When to send a worker again:** when the user asks for more options, or for something nicer or simpler, or has turned down every candidate. **Why:** technical spec 5.2's rejection bullet already says a worker is needed only when none are left or the user asks for more. It needed to be in the prompt now that there are workers. Written into technical spec 5.2.

- **What the coordinator does with a worker's result.** It tells the user briefly what was found, recommends where it helps, doesn't list every candidate (the option card shows them), raises the problems, asks the questions, and offers choices when a stop got nothing. The instructions also say what each part of the result means. **Why:** tool design section 4 says the instructions explain a reply's lines, and the meal coverage answer says the coordinator tells the user when a worker found nothing. Written into technical spec 5.2.

- **Until the leg scout, stops along a leg or near the start or end place get no worker.** The coordinator leaves them empty, and tells the user they can name a place. **Why:** the meal default puts lunch along the leg on driving days, and the coordinator has no worker for it yet. Without the line, it might send the stay researcher for them, and `search_near` refuses a stop along the leg. #61 replaces the line (added to its Do). Written into technical spec 5.2.

- **The meal coverage answer is now in the design and the prompt.** The settled question said to write it into technical spec 5.2, under laying out a day, and functional spec 7.3. Neither had it, so this PR adds both, and the "Laying out days" section of the prompt.

- **Hours for a place found on the web come from `search_near`, searched by name.** `find_place` gives no hours or rating, and the stay researcher has no `read_place`. **Why:** this uses the tools as they are, and `search_near` gives hours on the stop's own date. Written into technical spec 6.1.

- **The stay researcher is told nobody reads its own messages,** so it keeps them short. **Why:** code builds the result from its calls (technical spec 6.5), so its text costs tokens and does nothing. Written into technical spec 6.1.

- **Two lines added after the chat check.** The Moab researcher offered the same Mexican places for two dinners, and reported it as a problem for the user to sort out. So the instructions now say to give each meal its own places, and to offer one place for two meals only when too few fit, and report it. It also put "Hours not confirmed" in a motel's notes, so the instructions now say hours are for stops only. **Why:** both came straight from the instructions as written. Written into technical spec 6.1.

- **The coordinator's view lists the worker types** under "Worker types", in the same line format Claude Code uses: "- stay-researcher: description (Tools: …)". The test builds it from the coordinator's `Agent(...)` entry and each named definition. `toolsOn()` moved to `src/agent/tool-names.ts`, since both definitions use it.
- **The rationale example drops "fits mid-range"** in domain model 3.9 and technical spec 7.2, as the settled question said. Technical spec 7.2 now says why: the card shows the tier.

prs.title: search_near drops places more than 100 miles away

description.text: Closes #233

- In `search_near`, drop results farther than the cutoff, 100 miles, before building the reply. A call whose results are all dropped says it found nothing near, as a search with no results does today.

- Change `search_near`'s description to say results that far away are left out, and that a query about a style alone, such as "Victorian house", can find little nearby, so naming the area can help. The implementer drafts the wording, and Joe reviews it in the PR.
- Update tool design 2.3 and the Google data source to match, and add the setting to technical spec section 10.
- Run `npm run agent-views`, and commit the workers' view files with the change.
- A test with a fake Google reply shows a far result dropped and a near one kept.
- `npm run check` passes.

- **A test with a fake Google reply shows a far result dropped and a near one kept.** Done. `src/tools/search-near-cutoff.test.ts` takes the saved hotels reply near San Luis Obispo and moves Apple Farm Inn to St. Augustine, Florida. The reply keeps La Quinta and Hotel San Luis Obispo, leaves out Apple Farm Inn, ends with "Left out: 1 place more than 100 miles away.", and saves only the two near places. A second test moves all three, and the reply says Google found no places, with "Left out: 3 places more than 100 miles away." Both tests fail on the code without the change.
- **`npm run check` passes.** Done: 125 test files, 921 tests.
Checked by hand: nothing. The change needs no database or live Google call.

decisions.text: 1. **The setting is "Near cutoff distance", `nearCutoffDistanceMiles`, 100 miles.** The value was settled in chat on 2026-10-30 (#233's struck-out open question). The name follows "Near distance" (`nearDistanceMiles`), so the two sit side by side in technical spec section 10 and in `settings.json`. It has no upper limit and no rule tying it to the near distance, since nothing breaks if it's set oddly. Written into technical spec section 10.

2. **Far places are dropped before they're saved.** The rejected-places filter needs the saved place IDs, but the distance check doesn't. Saving places no worker ever sees would only fill the trip's place table. So a dropped place never gets a place ID. Written into tool design 2.3.

3. **The reply says how many places were left out, as for rejected places.** Example: "Left out: 6 places more than 100 miles away." It uses the same last line `search_along_leg` uses for its end-distance drops. The count tells the worker its query drifted, so it knows to name the area, as the description suggests. Written into tool design 2.3.

4. **When every place is dropped, the first line is the same as a search with no results.** It reads "Google found no places for "q" around San Luis Obispo (place_…).", then the "Left out" line. "Around" already means near the point, so the line is still true, and it matches the issue's "as a search with no results does today". It isn't an error. Written into tool design 2.3.

5. **The description wording** (Joe reviews it here): "Places more than 100 miles away in a straight line are left out. A query about a style alone, such as "Victorian house", can find little nearby, since Google matches it anywhere. Then naming the area in the query, such as "Victorian house inn Portland Maine", can help." It goes right after the sentence about naming a farther place. "In a straight line" matches the description's own words for the distance it gives. It says "then", so naming the area is a fallback, not the default. The issue's Why says the best place is often in the next town, which a town in the query would push down.

6. **The Google doc gets a new row in its known quirks table (2.4),** with the Portland and Bar Harbor numbers from the issue. The Text Search row in 2.1 now says a style-only query can find places across the country, and that the tool drops them.

7. **The search_near tests are now in two files, and their shared helpers are in `src/tools/search-near-tool.fake.ts`.** The new tests pushed `search-near-tool.test.ts` past the 300-line limit. The cutoff tests are in `search-near-cutoff.test.ts`. The fake's `moved()` moves places in a saved Google reply by position, not by name. Fake files can't import Zod, and moving by position needs no parsing.

8. **The existing start-place test now moves the saved tri-tip places to San Francisco.** That test searched around San Francisco with places from San Luis Obispo, about 190 miles away. The cutoff now drops them, so the test would no longer see the hours line it checks.
